desc:
The road keeps going east and west. A very sizable hill can be seen off in the
west. To the south, the trees gradually give way to fields, and to the north, a
thick hedgerow obstructs movement. The dirt on the road is smooth and firm from
constant foot, hoof, and cart travel.
name: Old East Road

desc:
The road turns gradually to the east and south. An approximately four hundred
feet tall hill to the west obscures the view. A pasture with rich green grass is
located at the foot of the hill to the west, while the hedgerow to the north
blocks further movement in that direction.
name: Old East Road

desc:
Between fields to the southeast and the foot of the Bree-hill to the northwest,
the road gently swings east and south. Wooden fences divide the fields into
small lots. Each field is growing a different crop, giving the landscape an
extremely vibrant colour. Due to regular use, the road's dirt is hard and
smooth.
name: Bend in the Old East Road

desc:
The road gently curves east and south. A sizable dike and a towering hedge that
appear to comprise Bree's natural defences run side by side to the west of the
road. While a field of vivid barley is neatly delineated by a wooden fence to
the southeast, the road is inching closer to the dike as it travels south.
name: Old East Road

desc:
The road's gentle eastward and southward curves become a humpback bridge that
spans the dike. Following the bridge, a big hedge has been cut to make room for
traffic as the road goes through. To the east is a little field with a fence
around it and oats growing there.
name: Small Bridge over a Dike

desc:
Green grass and a few plants dot the ground of the pasture. The hedge that
delineates Bree's eastern border begins to grow tremendously thick and tall to
the west. A road does progressively curve around the base of Bree-hill to the
east and south.
name: Foot of Bree-hill

desc:
The road stretches east and west. To the east, the Bree gate can be spotted.
Westbound lies the trade district of Bree before arriving at central Bree, and
houses line the street to the north and south. The noise and the hustle and
bustle of the city seems to be much quieter here.
name: Old East Road

desc:
The street continues to stretch to the east and the west, packed firm underfoot
by heavy foot and hoof traffic. North lies several houses tightly cramped
together, while to the south the noise of metalworkers can be heard. The Bree
gate can be seen off in the distance to the east.
name: Old East Road

desc:
A wide space opens up before the smith's working area to the south, plenty of
space for wagons both to deliver and haul off weapons, arrows and armour for
buyers. The white sand packed street is divided with poles and ropes to allow a
good flow of visitors to pass the wagons parked.
name: Metalworker's Bend

desc:
The street of white sand and gravel widens towards the south, coming to a large
bend. Houses align the street both to the east and west, with about six yards
between them. A dark and narrow alley winds its way west between some of the
shops, contrasting the bright blue and pretty shop to the east.
name: Old East Road

desc:
Slightly narrowing to the north and wider towards the south, the road passes
between houses on either side. White sand with stones of marbled white and black
make the road surface nicely packed over years of use. From the west a constant
smell of baked goods fills the street.
name: Old East Road

desc:
The Old East Road travels north and south here, and is about three yards wide.
This nicely maintained road goes into the trade district in Bree. Several houses
on either side flank the road, their colours contrasting the white gravel and
sand used to make an entirely flat road.
name: Old East Road

desc:
This wide space has become the natural travelling hub of Bree. From the north
music flows, and the pleasant smell of fresh food beckons. The Old East Road
comes from the west and continues south through the village. The Prancing Pony
Inn lies to the north.
name: Sign of the Prancing Pony Inn

desc:
A large front room opens up, where the inn divides further. North lies the
foyer, where rooms can be rented, and west lies the bar, common room, and game
room. The walls and floor are all solid timber frames, clad with wide planks
painted in a pale blue shade on the walls. A few benches for seating stand along
the eastern wall, where the view through a few small windows show the Bree
stables.
name: Prancing Pony Inn

desc:
A risen plateau in the northern part of the Prancing Pony Inn, accessed through
a rounded opening from the south, is where the deals for rented lodging are
made. From here a few rooms can be seen down a corridor, and several stairs lead
into other corridors upstairs.
name: Lodging Foyer

desc:
The Cobble Street narrows going west to east, almost twice as wide towards the
large plaza to the west than continuing east. A large portion of the narrowing
is the entrance to a tall stable north, built onto the large stone slabs the
street is built from.
name: Cobble Street

desc:
As the street made from large stone slabs packed with dirt between them sharply
bends, it intersects with a smaller road heading north. Towards the south the
Cobble Street continues with a small incline towards a tall tower to the south
east.
name: Cobble Street

desc:
The ground is made from packed dirt over years of travelling, with a cover of
sawdust and ground rind from pine trees. The width of the road varies, wider to
the south but narrows slightly as it winds north up a gentle hill. Buildings
accompany the road on both sides, and east lies a large open archery range.
name: Mill Road

desc:
As the road traverses slightly up towards the north it widens, the layer of
sawdust and ground rind on the road is thick and bounces slightly when travelled
upon. It passed between houses on the east side and a man height fence to the
west. Between the posts on the fence one can see a large animal market. Down a
slight descent to the south, the road leads between the stables of Bree and an
archer range.
name: Mill Road

desc:
The road is narrowing both south and west from here, the bend in the Mill Road
is over thirty yards wide. All along the northern part of the road stacks of
untreated logs occupy most of the space, with just enough passing space to pass
by the loggers' cabins and get to the Bree sawmill. A house with several furs
hanging outside is seen to the east.
name: Wide Part of Mill Road

desc:
Passing between stone walls both west and south and wooden houses northeast, the
Cobble Street sharply bends. The stone walls along the southern border stretch
several stories up into the air. Nearby east, a park can be seen. Down a decline
northbound, a stone road, a dirt road and a large stable can be spotted in the
distance.
name: Sharp Bend in the Cobble Street

desc:
This park provides a quiet respite from the noise of the city. The grass is
well-manicured, with some low rolling highs sprawling in every direction. A
short path connects the street to a clearing in the grass here. A multitude of
insects teem the grass, feeding on scraps left by city residents. Linked with
the wall to the east, a tower rises to the south.
name: Tranquil Grassy Park

desc:
Paved with large stones, the Old East Road passes between the walls of the
Prancing Pony inn and tall houses. A pleasant smell of food accompanied by the
noise of people come from the northeast. Straight to the east the road spreads
out to a wide space with a large fountain.
name: Old East Road

desc:
Narrowing slightly, the Old East Road runs both east and west, still a wide
enough road for two wagons to pass each other. North of the road the Bree-hill
rises up, winding through the landscape. Several doors painted in rich colours
are spread out in the hills. South, an open yard spreads out towards a wooden
house.
name: Old East Road

desc:
Winding both east and south, the Old East Road has been paved with large stones,
giving echoes from nearby buildings when horses and wagons pass by. Heading
north, a white gravelled road winds its way upwards into the Bree hills. To the
east several buildings and most prominently the Prancing Pony Inn can be seen.
name: Old East Road

desc:
The wide paved Old East Road continues both west and north from here, and a
narrower Road intersects from the south. To the east a tall fence rises far
overhead, even while mounted. Several buildings can be seen down the south
street, and northwest a stone tower can be seen in the distance.
name: Old East Road

desc:
A narrower stretch of the paved Old East Road, passing between a steeply rising
hill to the north and houses to the south. Any noise here is echoed back from
both directions creating a cacophony of sounds. Westwards the road continues
towards the west gate of Bree.
name: Old East Road

desc:
The room is dimly lit, the only light coming from the blazing fireplace, and a
few lamps hanging from the rafters. The bar is just to the right of the
entrance, and a sign has been posted on a pillar beside it. On a good day, this
room is filled with all sorts of travellers and residents of Bree, and many
races can be picked out of the crowds. At times, it can be hard to see in this
room through all the smoke and poor lighting conditions. Behind the bar hangs a
large painting of Bree city.
name: The Prancing Pony Lounge

desc:
This is the main room of the Prancing Pony Inn. A big table dominates the decor,
sitting in the middle of the room surrounded by many smaller tables and chairs.
Often this is the place to witness hobbits, foreigners, and the inhabitants of
Bree talk loudly of the events happening in even the farthest regions of
Middle-earth. Those that rest here long enough may catch snatches of
conversations about faraway places such as Fornost, Rivendell, Tharbad, the Grey
Havens, Moria, and even about the unnamed Shadow that grows in the East.
name: The Common Room

desc:
A small inner room, more silent than the other sitting rooms of the Prancing
Pony Inn, offers some peace and solitude. Four comfortable chairs are set up
beside two tables made to play each other in games. Through a window set high in
the northern wall, Bree-hill can be seen winding north and west. Noise and smell
of food comes in from the east.
name: Game Room

desc:
Equally tall as the neighbouring inn, the stables of Bree are large enough to
house animals of all travellers coming through. Both west and east, eight foot
tall stalls for animals cover the entire side. Above each stall a roof holding
food, equipment and tools for the trade is stored. South through an almost
twenty foot tall opening, a wide stone road can be seen. North lies a separate
market for trading animals.
name: Towering Stable

desc:
A dirt-packed plaza spreads out, housing several stalls and small stables
housing animals for sale. Tenders and owners occupy their own, all deals here
are made through one broker. On the southern end, a tall opening leads into the
Bree stables, and a passing road can be seen north. The fence on the eastern
side shows a large sign and an advisory on pets.
name: Animal Market

desc:
With a slight descent going west from the wide bend in the east, the road winds
its way past an animal market to the south. Packed dirt makes most of the road,
with bits covered in sawdust and rind. Towards the west the road progressively
turns more stone and gravel. In the western horizon the Bree-hill spreads out,
with peaks and valleys en masse.
name: Mill Road

desc:
Enclosed on the southern and eastern side, with thick logs of standing pine to
the south and thinner wood with stone behind to the east. Along the eastern
wall, six large targets made from packed straw stand out with their painted red
circlular stripes. On the ground, immersed white logs mark out three different
distances to the targets.
name: Archery Range

desc:
Turning north and east, the rough road of stone and gravel travels through a dip
in the terrain. A steep hill towards the west bars any climb into the Bree hills
and sliding track attempts to climb can be seen. The road continues northbound
towards a suburb of Bree and east towards the sawmill and the rest of Bree.
name: Stone Road

desc:
As the coarse stone road narrows amply, it passes through an opening in a stone
wall. The massive stone wall coming from the east decreases in height, being
over ten feet on the east end and like a three foot fence when it carries on
west into Bree-hill.
name: Stone Passage

desc:
A wide pathway covered in sawdust and rind passes south and east outside four
equal timber cabins. The cabins hold temporary lodging for all the woodworkers
tending the Bree sawmill when they are not out foresting. The doors are all
locked, but a steady stream of smoke rises from all cabins showing their
occupancy.
name: At the Woodworkers' Cabins

desc:
The small and dirty path leads around a few corners and ends in front of three
houses. Most windows here are protected by wooden folding shutters, whereas many
doors were repaired more than once with thin beams. A few barrels with rusty
hoops here are obviously used to collect water that drips from rooftops during
rain. The alleyway continues westward.
name: Narrow Alley between Wooden Houses

desc:
Tall stone walls form the perimeter of this wide alleyway. The brick walkway
here is unkempt and uneven, forming a tripping hazard for unwary travellers. The
alley continues to the east, where it constricts as the buildings draw nearer. A
road can be seen to the west.
name: Wide Brick Alleyway

desc:
The stone wall to the west echoes all sounds, down to the most silent whisper.
The road is made from large stones stacked together, with dirt and sand
supporting them. Looking north, Bree-hill stretches out upwards with several
buildings in the far distance. South, the road comes up to a bend.
name: Mason Road

desc:
Stretching fairly straight down south from the Old East Road, this road made
from large stones packed together with dirt passes between several houses on
either side. A coach timetable hangs on a tall eastern wall. A bench provides
rest for tired travellers.
name: Mason Road

desc:
The stone road bends sharply here, neatly cut between the buildings. To the
east, a tall and dark building looms on the street corner, the chattering of
loud voices heard within. Slightly downhill to the west lies the city cemetery
besides a large wooden building.
name: Mason Road

desc:
Only four large stones stacked together make the width of the road, a narrow
five feet between the building to the north and a stone wall to the south. To
the east the road turns northbound where a large dark building dominates the
corner. Westwards lies the city cemetery and several buildings.
name: Mason Road

desc:
The stone road is wide and dusty, and ruts are etched into the stone, cut there
over time by wagon wheels and animal hooves. To the north, the road winds toward
the heart of the city. To the south, many buildings of different shapes and
sizes dot the landscape, where residents of Bree have made their homes.
name: Mason Road

desc:
Long stones have been embedded in the dirt here reminiscent of a cobblestone
road, though less sophisticated. A low wooden rail about a foot high flanks the
street on either side. The houses here seem to be all made from rough wooden
boards discoloured from the winds and rain.
name: South Mason Road

desc:
A well-crafted stretch of stone road stretches north and south here. Each stone
has been carefully cut, leaving only enough room for a few small weeds to peek
through the gaps. A small dirt path follows the road on either side, evidently
trod down by those not wishing to be run over by wagons and carriages.
name: South Mason Road

desc:
This road is paved with finely cut blocks of grey stone. Shallow trenches. been
dug a few inches deep on either side of the thoroughfare to allow the storm
water to flow away without damaging the street. Some of the slabs are covered
with patches of thick, green moss.
name: South Mason Road

desc:
Moss covers most of the rocks lining this section of the street. The stone-paved
road is cracked and weathered, with small tufts of grass sprouting up in various
spots. To the west, a line of hedges can just be seen between the rows of
houses.
name: South Mason Road

desc:
The ground here rises and falls gently. A thick layer of grass and small plants
dominates the area with small patches of dirt appearing here and there. A small
path of bare dirt winds its way between mounds and divots. A small circle of
stones surrounds the charred earth of a camp fire.
name: Hilly Glade

desc:
The wooden floorboards here are slightly warped and grimy, and care must be
taken not to slip. The air is slightly damp and smells of mildew. Wooden walls
frame this room in all directions but west. The ceiling is low and warped like
the floorboards, but provides enough height for the guards to gather needed
refreshment.
name: Guard Watering Hole

desc:
The inner part of the guards' mess hall is a large kitchen, where food is being
prepared for duty-fulfilling men and women. Several long tables are placed with
benches for seating and all the benches are covered with grey and black wolf
furs. A braided thick rug covers the room in all directions, and the walls are
fully covered with red and golden wool drapes.
name: Mess Hall

desc:
Along the northern and western stone wall, shelves and hooks for storing the
guards' equipment are spread equally. The guards' ready room, where they can
talk freely, play games, and spend a few minutes on break, is solidly built from
stone and wood. A rug of thick braided reeds covers almost the entire room to
dampen noise and soak up moisture.
name: Guards' Station

desc:
The base of the tower guarding the east gate of Bree is made from large stones,
stacked up high into the air and reinforced with metal plates and sacks of dirt
against the south and east walls. Along the east wall a stone staircase rises
into a level above, and west several rooms can be seen, spreading a pleasant
aroma of food cooking.
name: Base of the Guard Tower

desc:
A wide landing in the middle of the stairs leading up spreads out west, a thick
wooden floor holding the office where the Bree guards are administered. The
southern wall in small maps of Bree and the surrounding areas. Along the eastern
wall the stairs lead down towards the east gate and up to the tower arms
storage.
name: Tower Administrative Office

desc:
A solid wooden landing covered with a thick reed rug spreads out from where the
stairs from the administrative office come up. Solid metal lockers are placed in
lines throughout, holding armour and weapons for the Bree guards. Any new guard
arriving for service is equipped here before heading out for their daily
station.
name: Tower Armament

desc:
About eleven feet in diameter, a round floor with a stone railing allows for a
view of the Bree eastern wilderness. Wild animals, travellers and disturbing
elements are under constant watch by vigilant guards, allowing a rapid response
to any threat. A light wooden hatch, with a solid metal handle, leads down into
the tower. Beside the hatch, a hole allows yelling alerts into the towers main
rooms.
name: Top of a Guard Tower

desc:
A small path to the north connects to a shallow pond here. The dirt surrounding
the pond is muddy and slick, and care must be taken not to fall into the water.
A stone wall lines the park to the south and a neatly curated hill creates a
natural barrier to the west. The northern path connects this pond to a park to
the north.
name: Small Pond

desc:
Grimy and dirty, this house stands out in the Bree eastern area. The dark wood
walls, covered in grime and dust, sport no painting or ornament. Tiny ridges
cover the warped wooden floor, the result of ill upkeep. The windows are
similarly grime-covered, and their frames are rotting, crumbling vestiges of
once intricate handiwork.
name: Bill Ferny's House

desc:
With exits both from the west and north, the armourer's large working area is
divided by a path through it. On the northwestern side the tools, benches and
anvils are placed, all worn yet well-kept. A large angular desk is placed to the
southeast, where armour, cloaks and shields for sale are placed and a few
special items are hung for display on the wall. Between the armour a wooden sign
with a notice is hung.
name: Armour Shop

desc:
The dirt is mostly packed flat, except in a few places where it has been dug
into mounds supporting pieces of metal. The metal, some new and fresh and some
remnants of armour and weapons, is being sorted and stacked for use. The
fletcher, armourer, and weaponsmith of Bree all use the metals from here for
their daily work.
name: Metalworker's Square

desc:
Several large anvils are the first things that catch the eyes when entering,
each longer than the smith is tall. The worn metal is gleaming of oil, and in
several places, pieces are missing where a hammer hit wrong. Two stone furnaces
blaze the room with heat, fuelled by air blowing over coal. A long counter
stands across the length of the room, not far from the door, and the weaponsmith
displays his wares safely behind it, perhaps fearing theft.
name: Weapon Shop

desc:
The walls of this brick room are covered in a thick layer of black soot, and the
floor is lined with trails of black ash and silver metal bits. The ceiling is
high here, allowing ample airflow for the smelting of iron and steel. A shop can
be seen to the east.
name: Metalworker's Forge

desc:
The long and narrow interior of this house rises almost two stories tall. Long
sticks, the straightest the Bree saw can deliver, stand tall along the southern
wall. Boxes of arrowheads come straight from the smith to the south, ready to be
made into arrows.
name: Fletcher's Workshop

desc:
A large room opens up, almost square in shape. The walls are all painted in a
bright blue colour, contrasting a red wooden floor. Large hooks on the wall
display various ropes, most used for construction and building work and some
with hooks for climbing. Tools to create ropes lie neatly placed and organised
on workbenches.
name: Rope Carver's Store

desc:
About twelve by twelve yards the park stretches, almost flat with round stones
parting walkways and patches for growing plants and herbs. The small fields of
dirt are nicely tended and watered, growing what is fit for each season. Two
small wooden houses stand on the eastern end, smoke is rising from one of them.
Near one of the planted patches a sign is placed.
name: Spice Shop

desc:
Baskets and boxes line up on shelves along the southern wall, some of them have
a lingering pungent smell. On the northern wall, larger items like sacks, water
skins and ropes are on display. The room is narrow with small alcoves on the
eastern side, clearly made for sleeping with pillows and covers ready. A yellow
note is hanging on both sides of the entrance.
name: Bazaar

desc:
Brightly lit and open, divided by long tables made for baking, the room is both
tall and wide. Along the northern wall, several furnaces, warmed by blazing hot
coals and wood, are ready for finalizing dough into the finest bread and
pastries. Placed against the southern wall, underneath a window, a counter shows
baked goods for sale with shelves of fresh bread behind it. A small sign with
text is on the counter.
name: Brightly Lit Bakery

desc:
This space is a comfortable tunnel-like hall. Although built into the ground,
this hobbit hole shows no signs of the dirty, oozy, muddy dwelling an
uncivilised being might abide in. This room shows that many hours of care and
work have been spent in order to make the place as comfortable as possible for
the owner and his guests. The wooden wall to the south has a small peephole
installed in it.
name: Tidy Hobbit Hole

desc:
Tall walls to the north and east and a sloping roof down south and west, create
an uneven house. The wooden floor has one long side to the north and three
shorter equal sides. Large carpets in rich blue and gold colours hang high,
matching the curtains on four wide windows. The inner window edges are painted
artistically showing flowers and growths from the Bree area.
name: Dainty Home

desc:
Bordered by a tall wooden fence on the western side and houses to the east, a
park-like yard spreads out. It is almost entirely flat, rare for the Bree area,
and the grass, flowers and water features seem well tended. Pathways made from
stone slates over white gravel travel outwards from the centre.
name: Open Yard

desc:
An enormous white fur is spread out on the floor, being over nine feet from head
to tail, and makes up the focal point. A whole row of chairs is stacked four in
height along the eastern wall and a large raised patio with a desk is centred at
the western wall, clearly a room used for teaching and meetings.
name: Ranger's Retreat

desc:
Rising from the Old East Road in the south this road traverses northbound in the
hillsides. Even being over ten feet wide it is by no means straight, but winds
its way towards some of the official offices of Bree further north. A small
valley opening westwards leads into an isolated garden further down.
name: Hill Road

desc:
Almost twelve feet wide, this road naturally follows the hills of Bree. It is
made from an almost white gravel, bordered on the sides with larger blocks of
the same stone. Eastwards you can see the roof of the Prancing Pony Inn, and a
door set between two windows in a hillside. To the west the Mayor of Bree and
other official services can be found.
name: Hill Road

desc:
The white gravelled road bordered with white stone blocks flows naturally though
Bree-hill, slightly narrowing where it intersects with an entrance to a large
grassy park to the east. Up on a hillside to the west the wooden wall of a large
house rising up with several ornamented windows is on display.
name: Hill Road

desc:
The white road is only seven feet wide passing through a simple yet sturdy
timber passage, going south it widens to twice that width. The stones framing
the road southbound stop before the passage, allowing the grass to grow close to
the gravel. On either side of the road the Bree-hill rises, creating a shaded
area. North of the passage the road narrows down to a trail made from white
gravel.
name: Hill Road Passage

desc:
A large wooden archway marks the entrance to the Westhill. The weathered
cobblestone streets are well-maintained, but starting to show their age. Houses
and cottages can be seen dotting the hillside to the north, while the larger
buildings of central Bree cover the landscape to the south.
name: Entrance to the Westhill

desc:
Both south and north, steep hillsides create a tranquil and secluded garden,
with a large flat area stretching in all directions. On the southern end of the
flat area a large tent has been erected, and rising up to the west a looming
tower dominates a nearby hilltop. A small opening between the hillsides leads to
a white road in the east.
name: Tranquil Garden

desc:
While grass is growing, this place is mostly covered in green. Most of the hill
is slanting upwards towards the west, before it tips downwards to the Bree
training grounds. When used only muffled sounds make it over the top, making the
grassy hill silent and restful. Sitting down here allows a pleasant rest, while
viewing the busy life of Bree swarm by to the southeast. A few chosen spots have
been used often, where flat areas allow for a campfire and eating a picnic. A
large house rises to the north, through a small opening a desk can be seen.
Heading down east leads to a road in the hills.
name: Bree-hill Park

desc:
Several old campfires can be seen around the hills, where they rise eastwards
towards a park for children. Over some hilltops southwards the roof of the
Prancing Pony Inn can be seen, the smoke from its chimneys crawl though the
bushes growing nearby. In the north hillside a large door with double windows
framed by two windows on each side stick out as a special home.
name: Bree-hill

desc:
With rolling hills rising in the north, east and south a natural flat and shaded
area is used as a city playground. Between two trees, a solid trunk of dark wood
has ropes with large knots hanging, and a long slide has been built into a steep
part of the eastern hillside. A few benches sit alongside a patch of fine sand,
where children's toys are scattered.
name: Hilly Playground

desc:
The cobblestones of Westhill Way wind between the northern knolls of Bree here.
A few houses have been built on the flatter portions of landscape, while other
homes are built directly into the hillside. To the south, the roof of the
Prancing Pony is just visible between the hills.
name: Westhill Way

desc:
The road narrows here as it passes between a few of the a few closely packed
houses, each slightly different than the last. The cobblestone streets are worn,
having seen the tread of many a foot over the years. The southwest side of the
street is marked by a giant pothole where some wagons have attempted to cut the
corner a few too many times.
name: Westhill Way

desc:
Only the four small windows near the top of the eastern and western stone wall
allow any natural light inside, while several torches hanging on the walls give
it a feeling of evening even during the day. Even the ceiling and the floor are
made from the same stone, the ceiling with a dome-shaped arch to support its
weight.
name: Shaded Stone Building

desc:
A northern wall in grey stone is contrasting the rest of this large office,
where all other walls are made from finely cut wooden planks painted brightly
yellow. Windows on three sides make it naturally lit while its day, through the
western window a fishing dock can be observed.
name: Bree Official Planning Office

desc:
In a drastic contrast to the dark exterior of this house, the inside is bright
both in colour and lighting. The windows have all been nailed shut from the
inside, with only suspended oil lanterns creating the light. A wide wooden
ladder leads up to a loft above, and a sign points down towards a gambling room
though a wooden cellarhatch.
name: Freebooters' Society

desc:
This simple room is walled with thick slabs of pine, and the rafters of its
sloped roof are exposed, giving the room a rustic feel. The floorboars are
similarly composed of pine, and are wide, smooth and without dimples or ridges.
The austere abode is heated warmly by a fireplace.
name: Clint's Small House

desc:
This oblong loft space has been decorated like a narrow street, being lit by a
lamp that looks like any street-lamp found in Bree. Mannequins representing
citizens and other travellers have been equipped with purses, handbags and other
resembling items that can be stolen.
name: Freebooters' Training Loft

desc:
A clear sign of dwarven masonry is seen on several of the stone blocks making up
the walls in this cellar, being carved with intricate scenes from battles. The
air here is thick with excitement and nervousness. It is not always large
amounts of money that are at stake; some people pay their gambling addiction
with their lives.
name: Gambling Basement

desc:
Halfway formed as a hobbit hole, with one and a half wall built from leftover
planks and timber, this burrow is small and narrow. Half of an old barrel make
the foot of a table with an old round door on top. Scattered around the room,
several empty bottles lie discarded, two bottles with candles in them seem to be
the only light source in the room.
name: A Hillside Burrow

desc:
Over fourteen feet in diameter this octagonal tent accommodates all features
needed for comfortable living. In the middle of the tent a large open fireplace
allows for cooking, the smoke rises slowly through an opening in the ceiling
nine feet above the ground. Two timber framed stands hold four hammocks for
sleeping, and a giant bear fur has been carefully put on a deep chair.
name: Heavy Wool Marquee

desc:
This large one-room, once a smial, has been cleverly rebuilt into a nice home
set in the lush Bree-hill. The western wall has two beds built into it, with
heavy woollen covers to draw. The roof is high and shaped like a dome, covered
with a bright red coloured clay. The entire northeastern corner is displaying
tools from a smith, framing a large furnace still able to give off pleasant
heat.
name: Secluded Hobbit Smial

desc:
Two rooms with an open hallway between them form this cosy hobbit home in
Bree-hill. All the walls have been covered with a dimmed pink colour, framed by
green-painted timber. The same green colour is on the round door and the window
frames. A large painting is hanging over a deeply inset fireplace. Smoke from
the fire is flowing out through a wide chimney.
name: Cosy Hobbit Hole

desc:
This is a long and narrow, yet tall room, built with standing flat planks on the
walls, floor and ceiling. The floor and walls are painted in a bright ochre
colour, with dark green patterns forming trees and a hedge around the room. A
large sign labelled 'Bounty' is hung between the windows on the eastern wall,
alongside a big poster reading 'Citizenship Information'. Outside the office's
south entrance, a large park spreads out, and north another office can be seen.
name: Mayor's Front Office

desc:
Three of the walls here are plain dark ochre-coloured, with the northern wall
featuring a red-painted pattern. A large stack of books in one corner supports a
ladder. The room's centrepiece is a gigantic four-armed cross hanging from the
ceiling, holding torches that light the room.
name: Mayor's Office

desc:
Over twenty feet wide a wooden roof covered in stone shingles covers the entire
training yard. A wooden horse meant to teach children riding, large plaques of
animals tracks and a wooden wall with attached metal spikes for climbing are
spread out, all made to teach wilderness skills. Some solid tents for living are
standing along the eastern wall.
name: Woodsman's Roofed Yard

desc:
A large open room with smaller compartments along the southern and northern
walls spreads out, with tools for the fur handling trade on benches and tables.
The compartments along the northern wall seem to be used for tanning and shaping
furs, while the southern ones are for coarser work like preservation, salting,
and unhairing. Suspended from the ceiling hangs a large skin, with red letters
on it like a sign.
name: Tanner's Workshop

desc:
Beautifully erected with white timber covered with dark brown planks on the
outside, this house is completely square in any direction. The white timber
creates a double cross on each wall, and a more intricate pattern of triangles
in the ceiling. A large open fireplace with a chimney is placed on the northern
wall, the chimney holds four large lanterns which light the room.
name: White Timber House

desc:
Over forty yards long, the roof over the saw is supported by logs every two
yards, each wide and solid and over four yards tall. Built as a larger copy of
the Old Mill in Hobbiton, yet here the water is used to power a saw. Studs and
planks for the Bree builders are being produced by sawyers daily.
name: Long Dusty Sawmill

desc:
Statues carved from wood stand tall in the shapes of wild horses dotting the
street. The flat, grassy road is bordered on either side by wooden planks laid
down neatly lengthwise. Wheel tracks can be seen having crushed the grass flat
going north and south.
name: Hummock Lane

desc:
The road here is composed of grayish white gravel with bits of red dirt leaking
out here and there. On either side of the road, rough wooden houses tower above,
their thatched roofs glistening with a hint of gold. A few fruit trees grow in
front of some of those houses.
name: Hummock Lane

desc:
A thick carpet of grass has broken free from its horizontal prison and begun a
desperate escape up the slightly sloped walls of the houses here. Gravel has
been kicked up here and there on the road and wooden planks have been placed
over a deep gash in the centre of the street.
name: Hummock Lane

desc:
Sludge-like mud has been splashed on some dark grey stones bordering the sides
of the lane. A trail of low bushes streaks along the centre of the street,
unscathed by the crushing, grinding wheels that have left indents in the mud.
name: Hummock Lane

desc:
Two large trees stand in the centre of the dirt road, their trunks acting as a
divide for passersby. The road itself is made up of a red, almost claylike dirt.
Looking closely there is a statue of a man standing between the two trees. He is
short and grey, and seems to be resting on a walking stick.
name: Oak Hill Road

desc:
The houses on this street all have decorative symbols burnt into their wooden
doors. Each is done with care, evidently the work of some local artisan. The
cobblestone street worn smooth, with and the East Road can just be glimpsed
between the buildings to the east.
name: Cobblestone Avenue

desc:
The tall oaks that give this street its name line the road on either side. A few
of these have faint figures carved into the bark, some with a few jagged
initials under the figures. The road itself is made from gravel packed with
earth and mud.
name: Oak Hill Road

desc:
The houses bordering the street seem to be rather low, featuring round doors and
windows. The doors are painted bright colours presenting a cosy appearance. Most
of these houses sport small patches of dirt in front of them, most likely used
for gardening.
name: Oak Hill Road

desc:
This private beauty salon is an establishment that offers a variety of cosmetic
treatments and cosmetic services for male or female of small stature such as
dwarves and hobbits. It is a place of tranquillity where ladies and gents of an
elitist circle come to get professional hair cuts and styling, manicures and
pedicures, and often cosmetics, makeup and makeovers. Several tools such as
scissors and combs or the famous heavy-duty toenail pliers are neatly organised
on a table set against a wall with a big mirror. A comfortable hairdressers'
chair sits in front of the table waiting for its next customer.
name: Curlybraid's Beauty Salon

desc:
Lush flowers and succulents populate this quaint courtyard. Small and cracked
cobblestones lead in snaking paths throughout the courtyard. Dried grass grows
among the cobblestones. Hanging vines grow along an arched entrance to the
south. Three stone benches surround an ornate fountain in the centre of the
courtyard.
name: Small Courtyard

desc:
A long, varnished bar runs from the northern wall toward the south in this dimly
lit tavern. Dark, stained wood lines the wall and the floor throughout this
room. Four small, round tables sit next to the bar with three stools around
each. Four stools sit under the long bar. Steel hooped oak barrels are stacked
behind the bar with taps installed. There is a stairway going up just behind the
opening behind the bar. There is an arched entrance to the east leading to the
garden courtyard outside.
name: The Taphouse

desc:
A large crystal chandelier brightly illuminates the main floor of the manor.
Well furnished with a dark navy blue rug overtop the smooth red oak floor, this
home provides sanctuary to fellow high standing compatriots of Robal. Etched
into the southern wall are stories of victories and friendships formed in a
multitude of languages. Bookshelves line the whole northern walls and are
subsequently filled with tomes, scrolls and flasks. Centre of the room stands a
large imperial staircase ascending to the second floor that leads to additional
bedchambers. At the other end, one can see shrubbery and greenery beginning to
form and coalesce with red oak almost in a natural way.
name: Elysian Sanctum

desc:
Crushed pebbles form a path in the garden leading from the east, then curving to
the south where it leads to a small hut. Flowers grow along the path in vibrant
colours and various sizes. A few bushes grow on the northern side of the garden,
behind a small rock garden. The rocks and stones all glisten with a shiny
finish.
name: Mahadewi's Garden

desc:
The high vaulted ceiling here in this room is adorned with a heavy crystal
chandelier which cast shadows of light upon the dark hardwood furniture. A long
table, made of rich mahogany, rests in the middle of the room. Surrounding it
are a set of matching chairs covered in lush red silk. Maps are strewn about the
table. Upon the maps are various models ranging from trolls to dragons. Large
tapestries hang gallantly from the walls, depicting scenes of battles of long
ago. At the far end of the table, a grand marble throne sits, engraved with the
past deeds of its owner.
name: Telolet's War Room

desc:
Though nestled within the walls of Bree, this hall shows a distinctly dwarven
architecture. Perhaps the owner, who has chosen to live in this city mostly of
men, was homesick for the comforts and customs of the dwarves. A large table in
the centre of the hall is laden with remains of a great feast. On the walls hang
rows of trophies taken from over which this home's owner was victorious. There
are several cots in one corner where the residents and guests may sleep. A
humble man stands here, ready to help you with your things.
name: Sonlayr's Hall

desc:
Hardly any sunlight can be admitted into this small and dank room. All of the
windows on the western side have been draped with heavy curtains, disallowing
any passer-by from Staddle Street even a glimpse from the interior. The wooden
walls have been decorated with numerous paintings of coins, jewellery, weapons
and artefacts.
name: Cebol's Shelter

desc:
This large room acts as a common area and a pathway that leads to additional
bedchambers. Unlike the foyer, this room is accompanied by a hearthstone in the
middle of the room that is burning providing a bit of warmth and serenity to
those that rest here. The polished red oak flooring signifies the delicacy of
the architect work to make sure that these halls remain for an eternity. Across
the eastern and western walls are commissioned paintings given by Ryalnos of
adventures from those that live within these walls.
name: Landing

desc:
Torches in silver sconces are fastened in each corner of this chamber made of
stone. The stones differ in light colours, forming a matching pattern on each
wall, with a brilliant white mortar between each stone. A bed stands along the
southern wall, with a small table on one side and two shelves fastened to the
wall on the other for scrolls, books and other trinkets.
name: Mieldor's Sanctuary

desc:
This room is filled with a peaceful aura. Bright walls and the white ceiling,
like almost everything in this room have been embellished with diamonds. Floor
is covered with a smooth, sky-blue carpet, dampening the footsteps. On the right
wall there is a nice window, with a view to a cosy garden filled with flowers.
There is a round table with some chairs in the left corner, and close to it a
big bed, welcoming to take a nap after hard day.
name: Gilgamel's Sanctuary

desc:
This great room, built into the bottom of the northern slope of Bree Hill, looks
very organised and well decorated. In a corner, there is a great view of a wide
variety of weapons and trophies of past battles. On the other side of the room,
there is a beautiful fireplace, emitting a nice calm pale glow, as the wood
inside crackles and burns, soothing the room with warmth.
name: Sapo's Smial

desc:
As you enter the hall you notice a dim light reflecting on the huge pillars made
of mahogany, in between which stand tall burgundy-coloured walls. A majestic
lush carpet covers the stone cold floor. An illustrious sword-shaped crest of
Eriador adorns the wall across the hall adjacent to the oil painting portraying
Esmer of Calenardhon, heroic ancestor of Dunlendings. A curved hallway to the
south leads toward the inner bedchamber.
name: Grand Hall of Eriador

desc:
In the western part of the room a handful of scented, black candles are lit on a
nightstand. At the centre of the chamber there is a bed suitable for a king,
covered by a great cave-bear fur. It looks very soft, inviting for a nap. Across
the nightstand is a jewel-encrusted wardrobe holding clothes, armour and other
necessities for the lord of the manor.
name: Palatial Bedchamber

desc:
Dark coloured carpeting serves the purpose of hiding the numerous stains which
have resulted from many a party here in this master chamber. An unmade bed sits
in the corner, tilted higher on one side than the other. Several small notches
have been made into the side of the oaken headboard. A large closet takes up a
lot of the space on the south side of the room, spilling its contents all over
the floor.
name: Simple Bedroom

desc:
This particular room looks like a study, with a small desk and matching chair
standing in one corner, covered with hundreds of pieces of paper with varying
degrees of unintelligable scribbles. The faint odour of something burning
lingers, although no flame or smoke are visible. The frame of a bed stands on
the opposite side of the desk, relatively clear of debris, with a small feather
mattress and blanket.
name: Ashep's Study Room

desc:
The light in this grand room seems to fade in and out as if in response to those
entering and exiting it. Several large paintings depicting great battles, long
since forgotten adorn the walls. To the right there is a fireplace, above which
hangs an extremely well-crafted painting of Galador the Lord of Dol Amroth
fighting fearsome beasts. At the very end of the room is a large window. From
its ledge one can look far out to the horizon and even see part of the Old East
Road.
name: Mantra's Tiny Chamber

desc:
A stunning staircase leads into the chamber below, seemingly made of the purest
of white marble. It apparently is of dwarven make. A crystal chandelier hangs
from the ceiling, while several trophies and various gleaming weapons of war
hang along the walls.
name: On a Descending Staircase

desc:
This vast cavern stretches several feet in every direction. The only exit is the
spiral stone stair case, rising up from the center of this circular underground
room. the surface of the floor, walls, and ceiling are covered in a glossy
smooth black marble. The craftsmanship is of such quality that the transitions
of the surfaces are indiscernible, an obvious sign that the stonework was
crafted by a master mason. Set in the floor at the bottom of the staircase is a
large mithril mural depicting a hammer crowned by 3 stars. Behind the staircase
is a four-poster bed composed of the bedrock itself, and topped by a thick
feather mattress. The posts stretch all the way to the ceiling, and carved into
them are many intricate designs of rose vines. These designs are likewise
comprised of mithril, embedded into the stone of the posts. The stone of the bed
is likewise covered with the same seamless black marble that covers the surfaces
in the rest of the room. Several Bookcases line the walls, and a large fireplace
is set into the wall at the foot of the bed.
name: Black Marble Cavern

desc:
An old gravel path worms its way around many well-kept zigzagging rows of
vegetables. Wooden sign posts are embedded at the beginning of each new row,
showing the various names of plants and herbs. At the very end of the enclosing
a patch of grass can be seen with colourful flowers blooming in random patches.
A clearly visible sign has been placed here stating: Please do not trample the
flowers.
name: An Old Garden

desc:
The walls have been strewn with countless maps depicting various scenes from all
around Arda. All of the furniture is sitting under a layer of random equipment
only an adventurer would need. Only the bed remains untouched and ready for a
weary traveller. A soft wooly carpet has been laid out on the floor, dyed into
forming a map of Bree and a large X where this address is.
name: A Cluttered House

desc:
A thick stone wall stretches far both north and south, framing a metal gate set
within. The dirt-packed road transitions into stone slabs before the gate, just
far enough to cover the area the gate moves when it opens. A tower looming above
the gate is the first sight of Bree travellers from the east see.
name: Outside the East Gate of Bree

desc:
Towards the east, a tall and thick stone wall stretches far both north and south
and deeply rooted in the wall, a hinged gate is set. An equal note is shown on
both sides of the gate. Linked with the wall, a tower rises to the north. A
paper note is attached to the gate.
name: East Gate of Bree
